newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus assembly dismisses president's arms charge.
newsitem.headline: Belarus assembly dismisses president's arms charge.

text.p: The leadership of the Belarus parliament dismissed as absurd on Monday accusations by hardline president Alexander Lukashenko that the assembly was preparing for armed rebellion.

In a weekend interview with Interfax-West news agency, Lukashenko said deputies opposing his version of a new constitution, were "looking into the possibility of buying weapons and creating their own security system".

He accused parliament of trying to create "another White House". That was a reference to the October 1993 rebellion by Russia's parliament against President Boris Yeltsin which ended with the Kremlin leader ordering tanks to fire on the assembly.
A spokeswoman for parliament chairman Semyon Sharetsky dismissed the charges as laughable. "If Lukashenko has the name of a single deputy who has acquired arms, let him name names."

Lukashenko, who openly expresses nostalgia for the Soviet era, has called a referendum on a new constitution granting him broader powers. He wants the vote to take place on November 7, anniversary of the 1917 Bolshevik revolution.

He ordered plebiscites on other issues - upholding capital punishment, banning private land ownership and changing the national holiday. Deputies called a referendum for November 24 on their own constitution, abolishing the post of president.
Lukashenko became Belarus's first post-Soviet president two years ago on a platform of fighting corruption and pressing for a union of some sort with neighbouring Russia.

Under his draft, the president may be elected for two five-year terms. Lukashenko told parliament he wanted to rule for 10 more years, an indication he intended to start a full new mandate if the proposal won approval.
Lukashenko's rule has become increasingly authoritarian.
Up to 200 people have been given short jail terms for taking part in mass demonstrations last spring against his signing of a pact that would create a "community" with Russia.

Russia's Interfax news agency reported that Lukashenko held "confidential" talks in Moscow at the weekend with security chief Alexander Lebed. Interfax quoted officials of Russia's Security Council as saying that the men discussed the long-term withdrawal of Russian troops still based in Belarus.

Lukashenko has also put the brakes on market reforms, saying the state should retain the leading role in the economy. On Tuesday, he is to hear a report from ministers on developing the Belarussian economy into the next century.
